title: The origin, history, and resistance architecture of an invasive urban malaria mosquito in Africa
methods: whole-genome sequencing and joint variant calling
resistance haplotype and copy-number amplification analysis

data_scope.invasion_topology: single South Asian introduction -> Djibouti bridgehead -> three onward fronts (Sudan; Ethiopia/Kenya; Yemen)
data_scope.resistance_mechanism: predominantly metabolic detoxification genes; resistance haplotypes and copy-number amplifications introduced from South Asia
data_scope.data_availability_statement: not confirmed in scraped metadata; article page returned HTTP 403 and Crossref record is empty on data/code availability

core_conclusion: Anopheles stephensi did not invade Africa through repeated independent introductions: 645 whole genomes from Africa, the Middle East, and Asia support a bridgehead scenario in which one South Asian introduction established a Djibouti population that seeded distinct fronts into Sudan, Ethiopia/Kenya, and Yemen, spreading at contrasting rates and along contrasting routes shaped by landscape topology. Insecticide resistance is predominantly metabolic, with resistance haplotypes and copy-number amplifications imported from South Asia rather than evolved in Africa, so the invasion arrived pre-adapted. A companion genomic resource makes ongoing surveillance of spread and resistance operational.
why_it_matters: Moves African malaria from a rural to an urban problem for an estimated 126 million city dwellers; a single bridgehead implies interceptable chokepoints rather than diffuse arrival; imported resistance means control programs cannot assume a susceptible slate at the front; dominance of metabolic detoxification shifts the intervention menu toward synergists, class rotation, and larval source management and makes copy-number variation an operational surveillance signal; ships as a reusable reference panel, not a one-off reconstruction.
why_nature: Settles a contested invasion-origin question with decisive continental-scale genomic data; couples evolutionary genomics directly to an acute global health emergency; delivers two independently significant results (invasion history and resistance architecture) that jointly explain spread and control failure; the landscape-topology finding generalizes beyond the species; and the companion resource converts the paper into ongoing public-health surveillance capacity.
